mappings.note: A project that reconstructs a family's or village's past from whatever sources are to hand - exactly LO-59's 'describe their use in the reconstruction of the history'. Not LO-65, which is about synthesising historical developments, not about gathering evidence.
Historians as detectives: the comparison rests on weighing evidence, which is how sources are used. Not CG-SST2 at goal level, because the specific outcome on sources covers it.

Ordering BCE and CE dates, converting to centuries and computing gaps between events is chronological synthesis of historical developments, the only outcome in the frame that reaches dating skills. Not LO-59, no source is examined.
A museum visit planned around what the exhibits are and what they show - working directly with material sources, hence LO-59. Not LO-60, since nothing is located on a map of India.
Invites an archaeologist or historian to explain the region's past and why it matters; the item is about who produces historical knowledge and from what, which is LO-59's subject.
Defines History as the discipline that studies the human past. That is the goal statement itself; LO-59 would be wrong because no source type is named, and no other outcome defines the subject.

Identifies the geologist among the specialists whose findings feed the study of the deep past - part of the chapter's survey of where historical evidence comes from. Not LO-57, which is about locating India's physical features on a map.
The palaeontologist and fossils: preserved remains are material evidence of the past, so this sits with the other 'which specialist, which evidence' items under LO-59.
The archaeologist excavating material remains is the literal archaeological source that LO-59 names first.
Defines a time line as events set in sequence - the chronological ordering of developments. Not LO-59: a time line is a way of arranging history, not a source of it.
A century as a hundred years; a unit of the chronological framework, mapped with the other dating items rather than with the source items.
A millennium as a thousand years - the larger unit of the same chronological framework.

The panchanga is an Indian almanac of astronomical tables, which is India's contribution in astronomy - named outright in LO-74. Not LO-65, because the question is about an Indian knowledge tradition, not about how time is reckoned in general.
Defines a source of history as any place, person, text or object that carries information about the past - the opening term of LO-59.
Classifies monuments and mounds as archaeological structures; a source-type identification, which is the first half of LO-59.
Excavation as the process that yields tools, figurines and pottery - how archaeological sources are obtained, so LO-59.
Folklore and genealogy as ORAL sources; the item tests discriminating among source types, which LO-59 asks for even though it names only the archaeological and literary kinds explicitly.
Foreign travelogues as literary sources - the 'literary' half of LO-59. Not LO-61, whose subject is the issues and personalities described inside such works, not their classification.
Paintings, sculptures and carved panels as artistic sources; another source-type discrimination within LO-59.
That historians consult and cross-check many sources is the 'describe their use' clause of LO-59, rather than any single source type.
The roughly 300,000-year span of Homo sapiens frames the growth of early human cultures, which LO-62 names. Not LO-65, since the item is a fact about early humans, not a dating exercise.
Control of fire as a turning point for early humans - a distinctive feature of early human culture under LO-62. Not LO-63, whose developments start with hunting-gathering and agriculture.
Rock paintings are both a record of early human life (LO-62) and the visual source through which we know it (LO-59). The item genuinely sits on that join, unlike the pure source-type questions.

The end of the last Ice Age about 12,000 years ago is the climatic turn that opened the way to settlement and agriculture - a broad development of the ancient period, so LO-63 rather than LO-62's cultural features.
Domestication of animals alongside cultivation: the beginning of agriculture that LO-63 names explicitly.
Why early farming communities settled by rivers - the step from foraging to settled agriculture, again LO-63. Not LO-57, since no Indian river has to be located.
Defines a hamlet, the smallest settlement form; settlement vocabulary belonging to the move from wandering to settled life that LO-63 covers.
Defines an era as a distinct stretch of history - a unit of the chronological framework, with the century and millennium items.
BCE as Before Common Era: the notation on which all the chapter's dating rests, so LO-65 rather than a source outcome.
Matches each discipline to the evidence it works on and picks archaeology with excavated remains - a source-type discrimination across all four specialists.
Recognises a chart of emperors' reigns in order as a time line; an application of the chronological framework rather than a source question.
Old photographs and relatives' memories treated as valid evidence for a family's past - the assertion is precisely that these count as sources, which is LO-59.
Finds the mis-classified source (rock paintings labelled oral) across archaeological, literary, oral and artistic types; the sharpest of the source-type items, and still LO-59.

Statement set on fire, pottery and which metal came first - features of early human culture and their sequence, so LO-62. Not LO-74, whose knowledge of metals is India's specific contribution, not the general prehistoric record.
Why early humans banded together - shelter, food and shared knowledge; a distinctive feature of early human society under LO-62, not a development of the ancient period.
Places 2001-2100 in the 21st century; a century-reckoning item, mapped with the other chronology questions.
How agriculture changed food-getting compared with hunting and gathering - the exact transition LO-63 names, and a different demand from the early-human-culture items under LO-62.
Newspapers as the source for the last two centuries; a source-type identification extended into recent history, so LO-59.
Rules out future climate prediction from what archaeologists study, testing the boundary of archaeological evidence - the 'describe their use' clause of LO-59.
